identity.name: The Advocate
identity.tag: No seat. No vote. Everything else.
identity.desc: You lead the campaign for tax fairness — the coalition outside the building, the argument inside it. Members carry the bills; you make them impossible to ignore.

intel._note: The weekly intel report. Each FACET is gated by the skill that would really buy it: Talk Story prices the chairs (live scheduling odds — rumor below `band`, honest band at `band`, exact odds + disposition at `exact` — folded in from the retired Whip Count skill 2026-08-14, since reading a chair's real disposition was always the same read as reading a coalition partner's), Procedure reads the clock (deadline warnings before they are one week out), Policy Brain puts the MEASURED hearing rate in print (it is always in the bill tooltip, but tooltips don't exist on touch). Rumor-tier odds are seeded per week+bill and may be off by one band — wrong on purpose; do not 'fix' the noise.

poles._note: Display grouping for the skill sheet — Disco groups skills under their parent attribute and colors them by it; ours group under the campaign function they serve. Order here is the order they render, and each pole's color lives in CSS as .p-<id>.

_skillsNote: skills.*.pole is WONK (inside/institutional), ORGANIZER (outside/movement) or BRIDGE (works both faces). As of 2026-08-14: Policy Brain + Procedure + Educator are wonk (3); Talk Story + Mobilizing + Base Building are organizer (3); BRIDGE IS NOW EMPTY (0) — Whip Count was retired and its chair-odds gate (`intel.odds.skill`) folded into Talk Story at the SAME thresholds (band=3/exact=5), since Whip Count's own description ('who's really with you, in the building and in the coalition') was always the same read as Talk Story's ('reading a person — a skeptical chair or a coalition partner, same skill either way'). `poles.bridge` is left defined but unused rather than deleted — renderHub already skips empty poles (`if (!ks.length) continue`), so the Bridge column simply doesn't render; a future skill can reclaim the pole without needing this note rewritten. Rhetoric was cut the same way one round earlier, into Talk Story's organizer slot — this is the same move applied to Whip Count's bridge slot, so Talk Story now single-handedly carries BOTH of Bridge's old jobs. MOBILIZING vs BASE BUILDING is the McAlevey distinction and the split is load-bearing, not flavor: mobilizing activates the already-convinced (spiky, breadth — it scales the rally), base building grows the coalition and develops leaders (slow, durability — it carries the conference hold-firm roll and the Grange on-the-record dare). Do not re-merge them into one 'organizing' stat; the whole teaching point is that turnout and durability are bought separately. NOTE: this note lives OUTSIDE the skills object on purpose — main.js does `Object.keys(data.skills)` to enumerate skill records, so a stray key INSIDE skills breaks every skill-grid render (learned the hard way, 2026-08-13).

fiscal.name: Policy Brain
fiscal.desc: Revenue estimates, fiscal notes, and whether the number on the page is real.

procedure.name: Procedure
procedure.desc: Referrals, deadlines, decking — what the rules quietly allow.

educator.name: Educator
educator.desc: Breaking a policy down until a legislator — or a brand-new advocate — actually gets it.

talkstory.name: Talk Story
talkstory.desc: Reading a person, and knowing who's really with you — a skeptical chair or a coalition partner, same skill either way.

mobilizing.name: Mobilizing
mobilizing.desc: Turning out the people already with you — how many bodies in the room, and how fast.

basebuilding.name: Base Building
basebuilding.desc: Growing the coalition and developing new leaders — whether anyone is still with you in week 14.

characters._note: Only external actors get names — people the player negotiates or contends with. The player's OWN campaign (staff, coalition) is deliberately faceless: narrative injections speak for it (dialogue node `speaker` omitted/null renders as unattributed prose via saidHtml's narration path), and its two 'Talk story' slots (`office`, `coalition`) point at a place/activity, not a person.
characters._souzaNote: Sen. Chris Souza is named in chairs.json (s-wam) and is the ONLY named character with no talk slot and no scene of his own. That is the point of w3-souza: House money you can walk up to, Senate money you cannot. He never speaks on screen — his scheduler, his committee members and a closed door speak for him. Do not add him to talkDefaults; a weekly 'talk to Souza' option would delete the whole premise.

rally.name: Hold a rally
rally.desc: Pack the rotunda. Sign-waving, testimony trainings, kūpuna in matching shirts.

scale._note: Mobilizing turns the SAME rally into a bigger, cheaper one — more support per point of skill, less political cost. Reuses the identical skill/per math as check mods (modOf), just applied to an action's effects instead of a roll.

rally.result: The rotunda echoes for an hour. A senator's aide films it from the balcony, expressionless. Coverage runs at six and ten.

voices.text: THIS is the building's real acoustics test. Let them hear who the budget is for.
Loud once is a headline. Ask who's still texting the group chat in March.

bench.name: Build the bench
bench.desc: House meeting, then another. The people testifying in April are the ones you train in February.
bench._note: The deliberately UNGLAMOROUS action. It hands back the smallest immediate number of any move — that is the teaching, not a balance bug. Base Building's payoff is not the support tick, it is the conference hold-firm roll and the Grange on-the-record dare in the endgame. A player who only ever rallies arrives at conference with nothing left to hold the line with. Do not 'fix' this by raising the support effect to match the rally.
bench.result: Eleven people in a living room in Kalihi, folding chairs, one whiteboard. Three of them will testify for the first time next month. None of it makes the news.

voices.text: This is the only line item that compounds. Everything else you do this session, you spend.
Eleven people. Try filling a rotunda with eleven people. Ask again in April, I suppose.

lobby.name: Work the building
lobby.desc: Office to office, floor by floor. Coffee, one-pagers, favors remembered.
lobby.result: Four offices, two commitments, one 'send me the language.' The building runs on exactly this.

voices.text: Read the room right and four offices remember your name in March. That's the whole skill.
Charming doesn't skip a single deadline. Track which ones you spent today talking instead of filing.

start.text: Ground rules while it's quiet. Each week you get the room — talk to whoever you want — and ONE real move: a rally or a walk through the building. And what you spend your weeks doing, you get better at doing. Weeks disappear faster than you think. Lateral, crossover, conference, gone.

voices.text: One move a week. Scarcity. Finally, a mechanic this campaign understands.
Then never waste it on a week where nobody's watching.

choices.label: "Understood."
choices.reply: Sleep this week. You won't later.

w1-opening._note: Grounded in ~/HawaiiAppleseed/snap-medicaid-timeline (repo dtomkatsu/Hawaii-Appleseed-website, medicaidData/snapData arrays) — federal HR1 SNAP/Medicaid cuts, all already in effect by this session's Jan 2027 start. Figures: SNAP-Ed eliminated 2025-10-01 (-$2.5M/yr); ABAWD work-req age 18-54→18-64 2026-10-01 hits 16,570 adults 55-64 + 10,303 households w/ teens 14-18; Medicaid narrower immigrant eligibility + 6-month (was 12) recert already dropped an est. 1,200-2,400 people. Refresh these if the timeline's data updates.

start.text: Session opens today under weight that wasn't here two years ago. Congress's HR1 already went through the safety net once: SNAP-Ed is gone — over $2.5 million a year the state used to spend on nutrition classes and farmers'-market programs. Work requirements now reach 16,570 adults age 55–64 and 10,300 households with teenagers who were exempt before. On Medicaid, narrower eligibility and twice-yearly recertification have already dropped an estimated 1,200 to 2,400 people from the rolls — not because they stopped qualifying, but because they missed a form. None of that shows up as a federal line item anymore. It shows up here: the Council on Revenues says $9.8 billion in general-fund taxes next year against a $10.6 billion budget. That gap was already there. This session, it has a name.

voices.text: Read the caseload numbers, not just the caseload story. 16,570 and 10,300 are Hawaiʻi's own numbers — DHS ran them, not a national estimate.
Every family that loses coverage over a missed form, not a change in income, just learned exactly how fragile 'eligible' really is. That's an organizing conversation, not just a caseload stat.

choices.label: "We lead with what Washington already took — SNAP-Ed, the caseload rolls. Then we show how to pay for it."
choices.reply: The choice sets the terms. The revenue bills aren't optional now — they're how the state answers a cut it didn't vote for.

choices.label: "We lead with the math. Nothing moves unless it balances."
choices.reply: The money chairs will love this. The coalition will want to know the math includes people.

choices.label: Say nothing. Look at the numbers again.
choices.reply: The numbers do not improve under observation. Pick the package — the calendar won't.

presser.text: Opening Day. Lei on every railing, three governors in the gallery — and the press set up on the makai steps, where your campaign has the 9 a.m. slot. One microphone, four minutes, every outlet in town. What's the message?

voices.text: Four minutes, every outlet in town. Read the room before you read the line.
Whatever you say, say it loud enough that the back row remembers it Monday.

choices.label: "Tax fairness, by name. The register pays more than the penthouse."
choices.reply: The crowd claps. Upstairs, two office doors close quietly. Grange, at the edge of the steps, writes one word on a legal pad.

choices.label: "Cost of living. Discipline. A budget that doesn't wobble."
choices.reply: Inside, the murmurs are approving. Somewhere on the sidewalk, a coalition text thread goes quiet.

choices.label: Four minutes of pure aloha — thank everyone, promise nothing.
choices.reply: Warm, safe, forgettable. Three offices call before lunch asking for 'whatever that one-pager was.'

start.speaker: kawaguchi
start.text: Kawaguchi doesn't look up from the committee referral sheet. "I schedule what can pass. The bills your people are carrying — I can hear one of them early, IF the ask is trimmed to something the floor survives. Or you keep the full number and wait for me to find a week. Maybe I find one."

voices.text: A trimmed bill that passes still moves real dollars. A poster that dies in committee moves none. Run the math before the ego does.
Trim it and the base watches you fold on the ask before the fight even starts. That costs more than $25M.
He said 'find a week.' Weeks are HIS. But a chair who names a date in front of a witness has spent something he can't unspend.

choices.label: Trim the ask. Get the early hearing.
choices.reply: "Smart." He initials the sheet. Your bill just got $25M/yr lighter — and a hearing date.

choices.label: Hold the number. "Find the week, chair."
choices.reply: A long pause. "Bold." It is not clear that 'bold' is a compliment on this floor.

choices.label: "Name the date, chair. In front of your team."

success.reply: He looks around the room, then at you, and writes a date on the referral sheet in pen. "February 14th. Don't make me regret the ink."

failure.reply: "In front of staff?" The sheet goes face-down. "I'll find a week." He will not find a week.

w2-kawaguchi._note: TWO-PART ART, the first in the game: the dialogue-level `art` (w2-finance, the Beretania breezeway) carries the approach, and the `office` node overrides it with w2-finance-office. renderNode reads `n.art || dlg.art`, so a node-level key is all this needs. THE PLAYER'S BILLS ARE NOT HEARD YET and must not be written as if they were — Finance's referral deadline is week 5 (chairs.json stages.h-fin) and the date Kawaguchi may have named in w1 is February 14th, which is week 5. Week 2 is a courtesy call, and its real job is to hand the player the Senate problem: `souza-intro` is set here and spent in w3-souza.

start.text: Fifteen minutes, his scheduler said, and she said it twice. So you wait in the breezeway where the trades come through, watching the courtyard fill and empty and fill. Ways and Means posted its hearing notices this morning; Finance posts tomorrow. Neither list has your bills on it. It is far too early for that to mean anything — which has never once stopped this hallway from reading it as though it did.

voices.text: Week two. Finance's referral deadline is week five. Nothing has gone wrong yet — the calendar hasn't even started being cruel.
He gave you fifteen minutes in week two. Chairs don't spend fifteen minutes on somebody they've already decided about.

choices.label: Bring the fiscal note. Fifteen minutes, one number.
choices.reply: You leave the binder in the bag and walk in with a single page.

choices.label: Bring the caseload pages. Fifteen minutes, one family.
choices.reply: Sixteen thousand five hundred and seventy adults, and one of them with a name and a district.

choices.label: Bring nothing. Let him say the first thing.
choices.reply: You go up empty-handed, which in this building is either confidence or a mistake, and nobody can tell which until afterward.

office.speaker: kawaguchi
office.text: He doesn't stand. "Sit. Your bills aren't on my notice this week, and I'd rather you heard that from me than from somebody downstairs with a theory." He turns his chair a few degrees toward the window. "Eight hundred and seventy-six measures came to Finance last session. I heard a fraction of them and I'm not apologizing for the fraction. You are not my problem." A pause, and this is the part he actually asked you up here for. "My problem is that whatever I hear, Ways and Means hears after me. And Chris Souza hasn't returned a call of mine since November."

voices.text: 876 referrals, and this committee hands back one of the two lowest hearing rates in the building. He isn't being dramatic, he's quoting his own workload.
He just drew you the route: Finance, then Ways and Means. A bill he hears is still a bill Souza can bury. Plan for two gates, not one.
"Hasn't returned a call since November" isn't a complaint, it's an offer. He wants something carried to the Senate that he can't be seen carrying.

choices.label: "Then tell me what Ways and Means needs to hear."
choices.reply: He writes two words on a legal pad, tears the sheet off and slides it across: FLOOR, NOT CEILING. "Souza doesn't care what your bill raises. He cares what it costs him in a bad year. Go answer that and don't tell him I said so."

choices.label: "Hear one of ours early, chair. I'll fill your room."
choices.reply: "Everybody fills my room." But he writes something down, which is more than he did in January.

choices.label: "Call him. From this office, while I'm sitting here."

success.reply: He looks at you a long moment, then picks up the desk phone. He does not get Souza. He gets a scheduler — and he uses the chair's voice on her, the one he has not once used on you. "Jon Kawaguchi. Put them on the calendar." He hangs up. "That is the entire favor. Don't spend it saying hello."

failure.reply: "In my own office?" He puts one hand flat on the desk, which is as close as this man comes to raising his voice. "When I want the Senate to know what I'm doing, I'll tell them myself."

w3-souza._note: NO BANNER YET — the dialogue renders fine without an `art` key. Souza never appears on screen and has no talk slot: his scheduler, his committee members and a closed door speak for him, which is the whole argument of the week (House money you can walk up to in a breezeway; Senate money you cannot). The red check reads `souza-intro` from w2-kawaguchi — a player who spent Kawaguchi's phone call gets +3 here, and a player who never got in his office is rolling this cold.

start.text: Money Committee Week. Ways and Means posts its notices Tuesday at four, and by twenty past, every advocate in the building has read them off a phone in the same hallway. You have called Souza's office six times. His scheduler is unfailingly warm, remembers your name without being told, and has nothing — not this week, not next, and the week after that is holding for the chair. Room 211 is the same koa as every other door on the floor. It is closed.

voices.text: Ways and Means is the last gate before conference and its deadline is week eleven. You have time. What you don't have is a way in.
Six calls and she still says your name warmly. That's a scheduler protecting a chair, not one brushing off a stranger — and the difference is worth something.
There are twelve other members on that committee, and not one of them has a scheduler holding weeks. A chair is not the only person in a room.

choices.label: Take whatever she offers. Any slot, any hour.
choices.reply: 7:40 on a Friday morning, three weeks out, fifteen minutes, subject to the chair's floor schedule. You take it and you write it in pen.

choices.label: Stop chasing the chair. Work the other twelve members.
choices.reply: Four offices in a day, two of them freshmen nobody has ever asked for anything. Thursday, a WAM member you have never met asks a question in a hearing that came straight off your one-pager.

choices.label: Catch him in the hallway when the notices post.

success.reply: Ninety seconds between the elevator and the stairwell, and he never once stops walking. But he answers. "Your problem isn't me. Your problem is the House sends me things in April and expects a miracle in May." The elevator takes him. You write the whole thing down on the back of the notice, standing up.

failure.reply: He is polite, which is worse. "Talk to my office." He is talking to somebody else before the sentence is finished, and you are standing in a hallway holding a notice you had already read.

start.speaker: grange
start.text: Grange finds you by the koa doors, all smiles. "Big session, yeah? Our members can live with a lot — but the conveyance thing reads like a tax on selling your own house. Help me help you: carve out everything under three million, we stay neutral. Testify friendly, even."

voices.text: The bill already exempts owner-occupied homes under the standard threshold — that's not spin, that's the bill text. Cite it and watch him improvise.
Neutral-to-friendly from the roundtable is a real asset. Just don't pay for it with language the base will notice missing.

choices.label: "It already exempts owner-occupied homes. Read the bill, Curtis."
choices.reply: The smile holds, one degree cooler. "Then our testimony will read the bill very... closely."

choices.label: "Send me your carve-out language. No promises."
choices.reply: "That's all I ask." It is never all he asks.

choices.label: "Say it at the hearing, then. On the record, under your own name."

success.reply: The smile finally goes. "We don't usually testify on the record this early." They don't testify at all. Your bill gets a hearing without a villain in the room.

failure.reply: "Happy to!" And he does — warmly, at length, in favor of a version of your bill that does not exist. The committee writes down HIS number.

start.text: Rumor from the tax department: the Council on Revenues may shave the forecast at its next meeting. If it's true, every bill with a price tag gets harder. The coalition wants to know the campaign's posture before the papers ask.

voices.text: A rumor isn't a motion. Nothing on the floor changes until the Council actually meets and votes the number.
The building is already reading your posture. Silence is a message too — make sure it's the one you mean.
'May shave the forecast' is not a number. Somewhere there is a worksheet with a number on it. Ask for the worksheet.

choices.label: Go public first: "This is exactly why we fix revenue."
choices.reply: You beat the rumor to the microphone. The clip travels. So does your name, attached to the word 'taxes.'

choices.label: Brief the steering committee quietly. Keep powder dry.
choices.reply: Doors close, voices lower. The building notices a campaign that can keep its own counsel.

choices.label: Say nothing yet. Ask the department for the actual worksheet.

success.reply: Three pages of tables. The shave is 0.4 percent, not the two the rumor grew on the way over. You walk into the steering meeting with the real number and watch the room recalibrate around you.

failure.reply: You quote a line from the wrong column at the wrong meeting. It is corrected, gently, by someone junior to you.

start.text: Health department's in the hallway with a real one: a federal reimbursement fell through and a rural clinic network needs a $40M emergency appropriation to stay open through the fiscal year. The rescue coalition wants your campaign's name on the joint letter by Friday.

voices.text: Forty million to keep the doors open in places with one doctor per island district. The network that shows up for you in March is built on days like this.
Every emergency signed off-cycle is a line item nobody voted on in the open. Ask where the forty comes FROM before you sign.

choices.label: Sign the letter. Clinics stay open.
choices.reply: Your campaign's name goes second on the list. The clinic director cries in the hallway. The fiscal note does not.

choices.label: Ask for a scrubbed budget first. Defer.
choices.reply: Prudent, defensible — and the neighbor-island papers run 'LAWMAKERS STALL CLINIC RESCUE' anyway.

start.text: Morning paper, page A1 turn: an op-ed titled 'The Last Tax Hike Hawaiʻi Can Afford,' signed by three retired executives. It names your bills. It is, annoyingly, well written.

voices.text: A well-written op-ed still gets the causation backwards. That's a teachable moment, if you can resist just yelling 'wrong.'
Three retired executives against school meals is a sentence that reads itself out loud. Consider letting it.

choices.label: Write the response yourself. Name the stakes, name the kids.
choices.reply: Your reply runs Sunday. The coalition shares it 400 times. One executive writes again; nobody reads the sequel.

choices.label: Let it breathe. Op-eds don't vote.
choices.reply: By Thursday it's fish wrap. The building respects a campaign that doesn't chase every ball.

choices.label: Skip the reply. Take it to live radio, unedited.

success.reply: Forty minutes, no filter, one host who lets you finish a sentence. By noon two of the three executives are being asked about THEIR taxes.

failure.reply: You are asked, four times, whether this is a tax increase. Four times you explain that it is complicated. The clip that travels is the fourth time.

start.text: Hearing day. Forty testifiers are signed up — teachers, a school cook, two ranchers, a hotel housekeeper with her whole shift outside. Two minutes each. The chair is already checking his watch. Somebody has to go first.

voices.text: The cook feeds four hundred kids a day. Put the number in the room, not just the argument.
The ranchers flip a room faster than anyone expects — 'small business supports this' still moves skeptics.

choices.label: The school cook goes first.
choices.reply: Two minutes, no notes. The chair stops checking his watch. Twitter does the rest.

choices.label: The ranchers go first.
choices.reply: 'We're not anti-business — we ARE the business.' Two committee skeptics visibly recalibrate.

choices.label: Neither. Fill the room past the sign-up sheet and let him try to gavel it.

success.reply: By 9:40 the overflow room is full and they open a second overflow room. The chair, on the record, extends testimony by ninety minutes. Nobody in that hallway forgets that they are the reason.

failure.reply: Twenty-two show. The overflow room stays dark and the chair caps testimony at forty minutes, politely. The housekeeper who took an unpaid morning off does not get called.

start.text: Friday coalition potluck, church hall two blocks makai of the Capitol. Someone brought squid lūʻau, someone brought Costco chicken bake, and somebody's cousin on Senate staff brought a rumor about conference chairs. Attendance is, technically, optional.

voices.text: Half the real deals of the decade get made over paper plates. Go. Bring something store-bought and humble.
Go — but work the room. The staff there know which bills are actually moving, three weeks before the papers do.

choices.label: Go. Eat. Listen twice as much as you talk.
choices.reply: You learn two referral rumors and one recipe. The week ends warmer than it started.

choices.label: Skip it. The inbox is a crime scene.
choices.reply: Productive, lonely. Monday, everyone else shares an inside joke about the chicken bake.

start.text: Sine die. Lei on the podiums again, and the building exhales all at once. Whatever you moved this session is moving; whatever you didn't is next January's problem. Interim starts tomorrow — that's when we count what it all did.

voices.text: Rest. Then back to the gap — it doesn't adjourn just because the building does.
Adequate. Nobody bankrupted the place, which around here counts as a triumph. Ask again in January whether it still does.

choices.label: Walk out through the rotunda one more time.
choices.reply: The Capitol is open to the sky in the middle — by design. Money in, money out, and the weather gets a vote too.

start.text: The whiteboard by the door hasn't changed: bills are alive until a deadline says otherwise. Lateral and crossover weeks are where they go to die quietly — spend the one action you get where a week actually turns.

voices.text: Deadlines don't care how busy the week was. Neither does the whiteboard.

choices.label: "Thanks. Back to it."
choices.reply: Someone's taped a fresh sticky note under the deadline column: DRINK WATER. SESSIONS ARE CARDIO.

start.speaker: kawaguchi
start.text: "Every advocate who makes it up these stairs thinks their bill is the one the ceiling bends for." He taps the referral sheet. "Bring me something the floor survives, and we'll talk about ceilings."

voices.text: The ceiling is a CHOICE. Someone typed it into a spreadsheet. Ask which one.
The man guards the referral sheet. You will need him more than he needs you.

choices.label: "Noted, chair."
choices.reply: He almost smiles. Almost.

start.speaker: grange
start.text: "Nothing personal, ever — that's the first rule of this hallway." He offers macadamia candy from a tin. "Our members just want predictability. Tax bills are weather. We sell umbrellas."

voices.text: Predictability IS worth money. He's the most honest person on this floor, in the way a price tag is honest.
Take the candy. Audit the metaphor. Weather doesn't hire three lobbyists per raindrop.

choices.label: Take the candy. Keep walking.
choices.reply: It's good candy. It is always good candy.

start.text: The coalition count on the wall: 61 orgs on the meals bill, 40 on the credit, 'it's complicated' scrawled next to anything with the word conveyance in it. One big turnout moment fits in a month — whoever asks early gets it.

voices.text: This is your actual caucus. The one that shows up in matching shirts.
Sixty-one organizations, one shared printer. Respect the logistics or lose the coalition to burnout.

choices.label: "Give us two weeks' notice, always."
choices.reply: Noted on the wall. Two weeks is apparently considered a luxury.

choices.label: "Forget the calendar. What does the coalition actually need?"

success.reply: The math on the wall stops for a second. Someone writes: SOMEBODY TO NOT DISAPPEAR IN APRIL. Under it, in smaller writing, three more things — none of them a rally.

failure.reply: Same answer as always: bodies at a hearing. You asked a real question in a hallway, which is where real questions go to be small talk.
